results.content: What is the difference between conda and Docker? The privilege needed to start docker containers is basically super-user level, making it inappropriate for shared computing environments with “ordinary” users who need access to the software there. The main difference between docker and conda is th. The main difference between docker and conda is that it can run on a specific environment. Conda and Docker solve different problems in reproducible software environments. Conda and Docker solve different problems in reproducible software environments. + You build a Docker image that contains a reproducible conda environment (best of both: conda manages packages inside a container that guarantees consistent OS-level dependencies). + Docker: write Dockerfile with minimal base image, copy environment.yml, conda install inside image; pin base image and package versions. + Conda environments are smaller than full container images; Docker images can be large—use multi-stage builds and slim base images. * Docker = container platform that packages complete runtime images including OS userspace (deployment-focused, higher isolation and reproducibility). Some Docker images use Conda as their primary dependency installation step, and there are now tools that auto-create Docker images based on Conda packages (see Mulled). results.title: What unit test coverage percentage should teams aim for? | TechTarget
results.content: * Software testing tools and techniques Part of: Unit testing best practices and frameworks # What unit test coverage percentage should teams aim for? Learn how to determine the amount of unit test coverage you need, what code to focus on, how to measure coverage and more. Teams can calculate statement coverage by dividing the number of code lines the unit tests execute by the number of executable lines of code. Most tools can provide this percentage, but teams can also use the following function to find their statement coverage percentage: **boolean two\_possible\_things(boolean thingA, boolean thingb) {** The function takes in two true/false statements, with the intention of executing a code related to one, both or neither based on their values. Here's the implementation in a bit more detail: **boolean two\_possible\_things(boolean thingA, boolean thingb) {** If both values are true, the code will work, and the single test will result in 100% statement coverage. If teams assume statement coverage as their testing standard, 100% will be extremely difficult to reach. Very high unit test coverage could be possible for new development, but none may be possible on older, poorly structured models. ## Statement coverage standards While there is no standard for unit testing, one number often cited in the testing world is 80%. If the coverage number is below 80%, and unit tests could reasonably resolve the incidents, it may be time to get those numbers up. Likewise, if the number is below 80%, but the team doesn't have problems that lead to rework or customer outage, there may be other priorities to work on right now besides focusing on unit tests. It can be a challenge to grow unit test coverage on an existing codebase. #### Dig Deeper on Software testing tools and techniques Part of: Unit testing best practices and frameworks How to plan unit test coverage Explore what an effective unit testing strategy looks like, whether it's wise to aim for a certain percentage of test coverage and how much unit testing is enough.
